title: Prometheus metrics in a Node service

story: Tuesday afternoon, Nova feels slow. A plan that usually takes five minutes is still running after twenty. Two explanations fit: Claude is answering slowly today, or Nova is stuck in a loop and calling Claude again and again. They need opposite responses, so you have to know which one it is.

Every one of Nova's model calls passes through the LLM gateway, our service that adds the Anthropic key to each call. So the gateway has seen the answer: how many calls, how many tokens, how long each one took. But it kept nothing. Each call came and went, and the only trace is a log line per call that nobody can add up in a hurry.
hook.question: How does a Node service keep count of how much and how fast, in a way that a dashboard can turn into an answer?

read.h: Count in the service, show the totals as text
p: The answer used across the industry comes from Prometheus, an open-source monitoring system, and its format is so simple you can read it. The service keeps a few numbers in memory and shows them at an address, by convention /metrics, as plain text. Each line is one series: a metric name, a set of labels in curly braces, and the current value. Above each metric, a HELP line says what it means and a TYPE line says what kind of number it is.

Two kinds matter most here. A counter only goes up: tokens so far, calls so far, dollars so far. It is never set and never goes down, except back to zero when the process restarts. A histogram answers "how long": instead of keeping every duration, it counts how many calls finished under each limit you chose, called buckets, plus a sum and a count. Below is the gateway's /metrics after ten pretend calls, from the lab. Read the bucket lines as "3 calls took 1 second or less, 9 took 5 or less, all 10 took 30 or less".

code.text:
# HELP ai_agents_llm_tokens_total Tokens through the gateway
# TYPE ai_agents_llm_tokens_total counter
ai_agents_llm_tokens_total{agent="nova",step="build",type="input"} 12000
ai_agents_llm_tokens_total{agent="nova",step="build",type="output"} 3000
# HELP ai_agents_llm_call_seconds Wall time of one model call
# TYPE ai_agents_llm_call_seconds histogram
ai_agents_llm_call_seconds_bucket{le="1",agent="nova"} 3
ai_agents_llm_call_seconds_bucket{le="5",agent="nova"} 9
ai_agents_llm_call_seconds_bucket{le="30",agent="nova"} 10
ai_agents_llm_call_seconds_bucket{le="+Inf",agent="nova"} 10
ai_agents_llm_call_seconds_sum{agent="nova"} 38.8
ai_agents_llm_call_seconds_count{agent="nova"} 10

notes.text: A counter. Its value is the total since the process started; the rate is computed later, by the database.
One series: the name plus one combination of labels. The type label splits input from output tokens.
le means less than or equal. Each bucket counts every call at or under its limit, so the numbers only grow from line to line.
+Inf catches everything, so it always equals the count.
The sum of all durations. Sum divided by count is the average, 3.88 seconds here.

p: In Node the library is @prometheus-io/client, the new name of the package that used to be called prom-client. You create a registry, which is the set of metrics one /metrics page shows, define each metric once at the top of a module with a name, a help text and its label names, and from then on the code that handles a call only says inc() or observe().

Notice what the service does not do: it never computes a rate or a percentile. It only counts. The database does the arithmetic later, over whatever time window you ask about. rate() turns an ever-growing counter into "per second over the last minute", and it knows what to do when the counter falls back to zero after a restart. histogram_quantile() estimates from the buckets the value that a given share of calls stayed under. In the lab, half of the calls stayed under about 2.3 seconds, but 95 out of 100 stayed under about 22, because one call in ten is slow. An average would have hidden that slow tail, and a slow tail is often the first sign of trouble.

code.file: the metrics part of the lab's gateway.mjs

notes.text: Our own registry instead of the library's global one, so a test can start from an empty one.
Counter names end in _total, and the unit or thing counted is in the name.
Label names are fixed here; the values come with each inc(). Every new combination of values is a new series to store.
Bucket limits in seconds. Put them where you would draw a line between fine and slow.
inc(labels, amount). The amount is the real token count from the response, not 1.
observe() drops one duration into the right buckets and adds it to the sum and the count.

read.see:
sum by (type) (rate(ai_agents_llm_tokens_total[1m]))  →  input 1200, output 300   (tokens per second)
histogram_quantile(0.5, …)   →  2.33 seconds
histogram_quantile(0.95, …)  →  22.5 seconds

deeper.h: Go deeper: labels are a budget
p: Every different combination of label values is one more series kept in memory and on disk. agent has a handful of values and step has nine, so they are cheap. A run label has a few hundred values a month, which is acceptable for the cost counter because cost per run is exactly what the weekly review asks. A label with a new value on every call, such as a call ID, makes one new series per call and slowly fills the database; the lab's fix shows it happening. A person's name or email is never a label, for privacy as much as for size: numbers are shown per team at most.

Who moves the numbers from the service to the database? With Prometheus, the database side does: a scraper visits every service's /metrics on a timer, every 30 seconds for example, and stores what it reads. That is called pull. It suits long-running services well: a service needs no database address and no credentials, and when the scraper cannot reach it, that failure itself is visible as a target that is down. On inf the scraper is VMAgent, which belongs to VictoriaMetrics, the Prometheus-compatible database we use, and a small object next to each service tells it which port and path to read.

Pull fails for one kind of program: a job that runs for two minutes at night. When the scraper comes by, the job is already gone. Such a job pushes instead: it sends its results once, as the same text lines, to the database's import endpoint, and it adds a timestamp to each line, so a result about last week lands on last week and not on the night the job ran. The values it pushes are usually finished numbers, such as a weekly median, not counters, so a dashboard shows them as they are and never wraps them in rate().

code.file: a push from a short job
code.text:
# a nightly job's result: one line, with the week it belongs to (ms since 1970)
delivery_review_wait_hours{team="fe",q="p50"} 9.5 1791763200000

# sent once, by the job, to VictoriaMetrics' import endpoint
curl --data-binary @week.txt https://<victoria-metrics>/api/v1/import/prometheus

notes.text: The same text format, plus a timestamp in milliseconds at the end: Monday 12 October 2026, 00:00 UTC.
One request, then the job exits. Nothing has to stay running for a scraper to find.

lab.title: Count model calls and let the database pull them
lab.goal: Add a counter and a histogram to a small Node service, expose /metrics, let VictoriaMetrics pull from it, and ask it for rates and percentiles.

guess.q: Your gateway counted 12000 input tokens since it started. It restarts, and the counter starts again from 0. What does a dashboard that shows rate(ai_agents_llm_tokens_total[1m]) do at the restart?

options.text: It shows a huge negative spike, because the counter dropped by 12000.
options.why: rate() knows that a counter never goes down, so a drop means a restart, and it counts from the new zero instead.

options.text: It keeps showing about the same tokens per second, with at most a small gap.
options.why: Counters are made for this: the service only counts, and rate() handles the reset. That is why you never compute rates in the service.

options.text: It shows 12000 tokens per second for one minute.
options.why: The old total is not added again. rate() looks at how the counter grows within the window.

follow.say: Make a small Node project and install the Prometheus client.
follow.do: mkdir -p ~/academy-labs/p6-2 && cd ~/academy-labs/p6-2 && npm init -y > /dev/null && npm pkg set type=module && npm install @prometheus-io/client@0.16.1
follow.see:

found 0 vulnerabilities

follow.say: Write the service: a counter for tokens, a histogram for call time, a pretend model call every second, and a /metrics page on port 9090.
Start it in this terminal and leave it running. Then, in a second terminal, read the page after about ten seconds.
follow.do: node gateway.mjs     # second terminal: curl -s localhost:9090/metrics | grep -v '^#'

follow.say: Start VictoriaMetrics with a scrape config that pulls your page every 10 seconds. host.docker.internal is how a container reaches your laptop.
follow.do:
cd ~/academy-labs/p6-2 && cat > scrape.yml <<'EOF'
scrape_configs:
  - job_name: gateway
    scrape_interval: 10s
    static_configs:
      - targets: ["host.docker.internal:9090"]
EOF
docker run -d --name vm -p 8428:8428 -v "$PWD/scrape.yml:/scrape.yml" victoriametrics/victoria-metrics:v1.154.0 -promscrape.config=/scrape.yml

…
(then a 64-character container ID)

follow.say: Ask VictoriaMetrics whether it can reach your service. A target that is up is the first thing to check when a dashboard is empty.
Wait a minute so there is history, then ask for tokens per second by type. The database computes the rate; your service only counted.
Ask for the time that half of the calls stay under, then 95 out of 100. Compare the two numbers.
follow.do: for q in 0.5 0.95; do curl -s localhost:8428/api/v1/query --data-urlencode "query=histogram_quantile($q, sum by (le) (rate(ai_agents_llm_call_seconds_bucket[1m])))" | jq -r '.data.result[0].value[1]'; done

follow.say: Now push, the way the nightly job does: one line with last Monday's timestamp, then read it back at that time.
follow.do: echo 'delivery_review_wait_hours{team="fe",q="p50"} 9.5 1791763200000' | curl -s -w '%{http_code}\n' --data-binary @- localhost:8428/api/v1/import/prometheus && sleep 3 && curl -s localhost:8428/api/v1/query --data-urlencode 'query=delivery_review_wait_hours' --data-urlencode 'time=2026-10-12T00:00:00Z' | jq -c '.data.result[0].value'

lab.build: The weekly review asks what Nova costs, not how many tokens it uses. Add a second counter, ai_agents_llm_cost_usd_total with the labels agent and step, and increase it on every pretend call by the call's price: 1200 input tokens at 4 dollars per million and 300 output tokens at 20 dollars per million. Restart gateway.mjs, wait a minute, and ask VictoriaMetrics for dollars per hour by step with sum by (step) (rate(ai_agents_llm_cost_usd_total[1m])) * 3600. It should say about 38.88 for build.
checks: curl localhost:9090/metrics shows the token counter, five bucket lines plus +Inf, a _sum and a _count
The targets query shows your service as up
The rate query returns about 1200 input and 300 output tokens per second
The 0.95 quantile is many times larger than the 0.5 quantile
After your build, the cost query returns about 38.88 dollars per hour for build
docker rm -f vm and Ctrl+C on gateway.mjs stop everything
lab.fix: A teammate wanted to find one slow call, so they added a call_id label to the token counter and passed crypto.randomUUID() on every call. Make the same change and restart. Count the token series twice, 30 seconds apart, with curl -s localhost:9090/metrics | grep -c '^ai_agents_llm_tokens_total': in our run it went from 8 to 68, and it never stops growing. Explain why, remove the label, and say where a single slow call should be recorded instead.
explain: Why does the service only count, and leave rate() and histogram_quantile() to the database?
Why did the 0.95 quantile tell you something that the average call time would have hidden?
The gateway is scraped, but the nightly metrics job pushes. What is different about the two programs, and why does a pushed line carry a timestamp?
lab.done: VictoriaMetrics pulled your service's counters and histogram, answered rates and percentiles from them, accepted one pushed point on last Monday, and you stopped the container and the service.

check.q: You want the gateway to report how long model calls take, so you can see a slow tail. What do you add?

options.text: A counter that you increase by the number of seconds of each call
options.why: That gives total seconds, and with a call counter an average, but no way to see that one call in ten is very slow.

options.text: A histogram with bucket limits around the times you care about
options.why: Buckets keep the shape of the durations, so the database can estimate the 95th percentile, where trouble shows first.

options.text: A label on the token counter with the call's duration
options.why: Every different duration becomes a new series. That is a cardinality problem, and it still cannot be summed into a percentile.

check.q: The nightly delivery job runs for two minutes at 02:20. How do its numbers reach VictoriaMetrics?

options.text: VMAgent scrapes the job's /metrics page every 30 seconds
options.why: The job is gone long before most scrapes. Pull only works for programs that stay running.

options.text: The job writes its numbers to a log file that Grafana reads
options.why: Grafana reads databases, not files on a runner that disappears after the job.

options.text: The job pushes its lines, each with a timestamp, to the import endpoint
options.why: A short job pushes once and exits. The timestamp puts each value on the week it describes.

check.q: Which label would you never add to ai_agents_llm_tokens_total?

options.why: Few values and very useful: it shows which step of a run used the tokens.

options.text: call_id, with a new value for every call
options.why: One new series per call fills the database and makes queries slow. Single calls belong in events, not in metric labels.

options.text: type, with input, output, cache_read and cache_write
options.why: Four values, and the cache-read share is computed from them.

p: The LLM gateway counts every call with @prometheus-io/client and shows the result on its own port, 9090, apart from the API on 8080, so the route the VMs use never exposes it. Its two counters are ai_agents_llm_tokens_total with agent, model, type and step, and ai_agents_llm_cost_usd_total with agent, model, jira, run and step. The cost comes from a price table per model and token type, and the gateway reads only the usage numbers of each response, never the text. The harness asks the gateway how much a run has spent, which the gateway answers from VictoriaMetrics, so the answer survives a restart.

On inf, VMAgent scrapes each agent service through a VMServiceScrape that comes with the shared chart. The nightly delivery-metrics job runs as a GitHub Actions workflow at 02:20 and pushes team-level series with timestamps to VictoriaMetrics' import endpoint, using the same metrics login that other workflows in the infrastructure repo already use.

tickets.why: The gateway's meter: token and cost counters with agent, model, run and step labels, on port 9090.
Deploys the gateway with a VMServiceScrape, so VMAgent pulls its metrics.
The nightly job's writer: Prometheus text lines with millisecond timestamps, pushed to the import endpoint.
The operations dashboard that queries these counters, including the cache-read share.

words.plain: One metric name with one combination of label values, and its value over time.
A number that only goes up, such as tokens so far. The database turns it into a rate.
Counts of how many observations fell under each chosen limit, plus their sum and count.
The database side reading a service's /metrics page on a timer. Also called pull.
How many different series a metric has. Every new label value adds one.

review.q: Write the four lines a counter needs in @prometheus-io/client, and the one line that increases it after a call.
review.a: new client.Counter({ name: "…_total", help: "…", labelNames: ["agent", "step", "type"], registers: [registry] }); then tokens.inc({ agent, step, type }, amount).

review.q: Explain to a teammate why the p95 of call time can be 22 seconds while the median is 2.
review.a: Most calls are fast, but a few are very slow. The median shows the typical call; the p95 shows the slow tail, which is where a stuck or overloaded system appears first.

review.q: When do you push instead of being scraped, and what must a pushed line carry?
review.a: When the program is short-lived, like a nightly job. Each line carries a timestamp, so the value lands on the time it describes.

remember: The service only counts, in counters and histograms on /metrics; the database pulls them and does the arithmetic, and only short jobs push, with timestamps.
